title: Want, can, like: verbs that hold hands with verbs
goal: Order food, turn down what you don't eat, and chain two verbs in one sentence — the second one keeps its *ku-*.
bekal: *ku-* as a noun: *kusoma ni kuzuri* (reading is good)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mgahawani
dialogs.intro: Budi's first dinner in a real restaurant, with Amina on hand as translator — but she isn't needed.

lines.speaker: Mhudumu:
lines.id: Welcome! What would you like to order?

lines.speaker: Mhudumu:
lines.text: Hii hapa. Leo tuna samaki, kuku na nyama choma.
lines.id: Here you are. Today we have fish, chicken, and grilled meat.
lines.literal: this at-here. today we-have fish, chicken and meat grilled.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ninataka kula samaki na wali wa nazi.
lines.id: I'd like to eat fish and coconut rice.
lines.literal: I-am-want to-eat fish and rice of coconut.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Naweza kupata kuku bila pilipili? Siwezi kula pilipili kali.
lines.id: Could I get the chicken without chili? I can't handle spicy chili.
lines.literal: I-can to-get chicken without chili? I-not-can to-eat chili hot.

lines.speaker: Mhudumu:
lines.id: Of course. What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na mimi napenda kujaribu juisi ya embe.
lines.id: And I'd like to try mango juice.
lines.literal: and I I-like to-try juice of mango.

lines.speaker: Mhudumu:
lines.text: Sawa. Chakula kitakuwa tayari baada ya dakika ishirini.
lines.id: Fine. The food will be ready in twenty minutes.
lines.literal: okay. food it-will-be ready after of minutes twenty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Asante. Kabla ya kula, choo kiko wapi?
lines.id: Thanks. Before we eat, where's the restroom?
lines.literal: thanks. before of eating, toilet it-is where?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Nyuma pale. Chakula hiki ni kitamu — utapenda!
lines.id: Back there. This food is delicious — you'll love it!
lines.literal: back there. food this is tasty — you-will-like!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kupika kwao ni kuzuri sana. Naomba bili, tafadhali!
lines.id: Their cooking is wonderful. The bill, please!
lines.literal: cooking of-them is good very. I-ask bill, please!

notes: **Naomba is the politest way to ask for anything.** Literally "I beg", and it works for things and actions alike: *Naomba maji* (water, please), *Naomba bili* (the bill, please), *Naomba kupita* (excuse me, let me through), *Naomba unisaidie* (please help me). If you could take only one polite word into a restaurant, take this one.

**Bila shaka means "without doubt", i.e. of course.** *Bila* means "without" and can be followed by a noun or a verb: *bila sukari* (without sugar), *bila pilipili* (without chili), *bila kusubiri* (without waiting), *bila shaka* (certainly).

**Nyama choma isn't just food, it's an occasion.** Goat or beef slow-grilled and eaten in a big group with *kachumbari* (a fresh salad-salsa of sliced tomato, onion, and lime). If you're invited *kwenda kula nyama choma*, it's an invitation to get together, not just to eat.

**Wali wa nazi is rice cooked in coconut milk** — a cousin of Southeast Asian coconut rice, and perhaps the most comforting dish on the East African coast. Its relatives are *mchuzi wa nazi* (coconut curry) and *samaki wa nazi*.

**Hii hapa means "here it is".** A demonstrative paired with a place word: *hii hapa* (here it is, N-class thing), *hiki hapa*, *huyu hapa* (here he/she is). A very common phrase when handing something over.

grammars.title: Two verbs in one sentence
body: When a sentence has two verbs, the **first is built in full** with subject prefix and tense slot, while the **second stays in its dictionary form** — with *ku-* intact in front. It's exactly the same as English "I want **to** eat".
after: Notice that **only the first verb is negated** — the second is untouched. *Siwezi kuja* (I can't come), not *siwezi siji*.

*Kujua* means "know" for facts and "know how" for skills: *Ninajua Kiswahili* (I know Swahili), *Ninajua kuendesha gari* (I can drive). Tell it apart from *kuweza*, which means can because circumstances allow: *Siwezi kuja leo* (I can't come today — not because I'm unable).

For a request gentler than *ninataka*, use **ningependa** ("I would like"): *Ningependa kuagiza* (I'd like to order), *Ningependa chai* (I'd like tea). Memorize it whole; its structure isn't taken apart until A2.

grammars.title: Ku- as a noun: "reading is good"
body: The *ku-* form isn't only "to…" — it also turns a verb into a **noun**, just like the English *-ing* in "reading is fun". And as a noun it has its own class, with the prefix **ku-**.
after: Three time-linkers to take away from this page: **kabla ya** (before), **baada ya** (after), and **bila** (without). All three are always followed by the *ku-* form, never by a built verb.

Look at *kwao* in the second row: the possessives for the *ku-* class are *kwangu*, *kwako*, *kwake*, *kwetu*, *kwenu*, *kwao* — exactly the same as the "at someone's place" forms you've used since unit 2. They're one family.
Swahili proverbs are almost always built on this pattern: *Kusoma ni kujua* (reading is knowing), *Kupanga ni kuchagua* (to plan is to choose), *Kuuliza si ujinga* (asking is not ignorance).

English
rows: What food do you have today?
When will the food be ready?

blocks.text: The last line isn't tech small talk: mobile payments (*M-Pesa* in Kenya, *Tigo Pesa* and *Mixx* in Tanzania) are used everywhere, even at roadside stalls. Your phone number is your wallet, and a sentence you'll often hear is *Nitume kwa namba hii* (send it to this number).
*Mgahawa* is a restaurant; *baa* sells drinks; *kibanda* is a small food stall; and *hoteli* — careful — in Tanzania often means a restaurant, not a place to stay.

sections.title: Ladha na maombi maalum — flavors and special requests

blocks.text: In Zanzibar and along the Tanzanian coast, most restaurants really are *halali* and serve no pork at all; in big cities like Dar es Salaam and Nairobi, asking first is a normal habit and offends no one. The sentence: *Chakula hiki ni halali?*

Look at *maji ya kunywa* — "water for drinking", using the *ku-* form from the previous page as a description. Same pattern: *chumba cha kulala* (bedroom), *chumba cha kulia* (dining room), *mashine ya kufulia* (washing machine). Swahili builds new terms from old parts, and now you can read them yourself.
